body_html:
Writing emails in Spanish is where many fluent speakers still feel unsure. Is Querido too personal? Do you need usted? Why do Spanish emails put a colon after the greeting? After years of translating business correspondence, I can tell you that a small set of patterns covers almost every situation. Here are the greetings, openings, requests and closings that sound natural, plus the literal translations that instantly give a learner away.

Key takeaways
  • Formal greeting: Estimado / Estimada + name, followed by a colon.
  • Informal greeting: Hola, Ana: or Hola, Ana,.
  • Open with your purpose: Le escribo para…
  • Close with Atentamente (formal) or Un saludo (neutral).
{{toc}}

Greetings: formal and informal

SpanishUse
Estimado señor López:Formal, to a man
Estimada Sra. Gómez:Formal, to a woman
Estimados señores:Formal, to a company or group
A quien corresponda:To whom it may concern
Buenos días, Carlos:Professional but warm
Hola, Ana:Informal or friendly colleague
Querida Lucía:Friends and family only

In formal Spanish, the greeting is followed by a colon, not a comma, and the email continues on a new line with a capital letter. The Diccionario panhispánico de dudas of the Real Academia Española recommends this use of the colon in letters. In informal emails many people use a comma, influenced by English, and that is widely accepted.

Opening lines for writing emails in Spanish

  • Le escribo para… I’m writing to… (formal)
  • Me pongo en contacto con usted para… I’m contacting you to… (formal)
  • En relación con su correo del día 5… Regarding your email of the 5th…
  • Gracias por su respuesta. Thank you for your reply.
  • Espero que se encuentre bien. I hope you are well.
  • Te escribo para contarte que… I’m writing to tell you that… (informal)
{{image:2}}

Making polite requests

Spanish politeness in writing relies on the conditional and on softening phrases:

SpanishEnglish
¿Podría enviarme el informe antes del viernes?Could you send me the report before Friday?
Le agradecería que me confirmara la fecha.I would be grateful if you could confirm the date.
¿Sería posible adelantar la reunión?Would it be possible to bring the meeting forward?
Quedo a la espera de su respuesta.I look forward to your reply.
Gracias de antemano.Thanks in advance.

Note Le agradecería que… takes the subjunctive (confirmara). If that feels hard, ¿Podría…? is always correct and polite.

Attachments, follow-ups and apologies

  • Le adjunto el contrato. / Adjunto le envío el contrato. Please find the contract attached.
  • Como le comenté… As I mentioned…
  • Le escribo para hacer seguimiento de… I’m writing to follow up on…
  • Disculpe la demora en responder. Sorry for the delay in replying.
  • Perdón por las molestias. Sorry for the inconvenience.

Closings

ClosingTone
Atentamente,Formal (“Yours sincerely”)
Saludos cordiales,Formal but friendly (“Kind regards”)
Un saludo, / Saludos,Neutral, very common
Quedo a su disposición.“I remain at your disposal”, before the closing
Un abrazo,Friendly colleagues and friends
Besos,Close friends and family only
{{image:3}}

Formal email template

Estimada Sra. Martínez:

Me pongo en contacto con usted para solicitar información sobre el curso de verano. ¿Podría indicarme las fechas y el precio?

Le agradecería que me enviara también el formulario de inscripción.

Quedo a la espera de su respuesta.

Atentamente,
Daniel Smith

Informal email template

Hola, Laura:

¿Qué tal todo? Te escribo para confirmar lo del sábado. ¿Te viene bien a las ocho en el restaurante de siempre?

Avísame cuando puedas.

Un abrazo,
Daniel

Calques that give learners away

As a translator, these are the patterns I correct most often. They are understandable but sound translated:

  • Espero que este correo le encuentre bien. A word-for-word copy of “I hope this email finds you well”. Natural: Espero que se encuentre bien.
  • Por favor encuentre adjunto… From “Please find attached”. Natural: Le adjunto…
  • Siéntase libre de contactarme. From “Feel free to contact me”. Natural: No dude en contactarme.
  • Querido in business. It sounds affectionate. Use Estimado.
  • Aplicar a un trabajo for “to apply for a job”. In standard Spanish, apply for a job is solicitar un puesto or postularse (Latin America).

Literal translation is a theme of its own; see {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|translating word for word: the mistakes to avoid}}.

Subject lines and signatures

Subject lines (el asunto) in Spanish are usually short and descriptive: Solicitud de información (Information request), Reunión del martes (Tuesday’s meeting), Factura n.º 245 (Invoice no. 245). Avoid writing the whole subject in capital letters, which reads as shouting.

A professional signature typically includes your name, position, company and phone number. If you work across languages, a short line such as Hablo inglés y español can be helpful for clients.

Replying to an email

  • Muchas gracias por su mensaje. Thank you very much for your message.
  • Con respecto a su pregunta… Regarding your question…
  • Le confirmo que… I can confirm that…
  • Lamentablemente, no será posible… Unfortunately, it won’t be possible…
  • Quedo atento / atenta a sus comentarios. I look forward to your comments.

Note that quedo atento agrees with the writer: a woman writes quedo atenta.

Tú or usted in emails?

Start with usted when writing to someone new, senior or outside your organisation. Many workplaces, especially in Spain and in younger companies, switch quickly to tú; follow the other person’s lead. If they reply with tú, you can mirror it. For spoken workplace Spanish, see {{link:talking-to-coworkers-in-spanish|talking to coworkers in Spanish}}.

Final thoughts

Writing emails in Spanish becomes easy once you have a handful of reliable patterns: a greeting with a colon, a clear purpose, a polite request in the conditional and a closing that matches the relationship. Keep these templates nearby and adjust the tone, and your emails will read as if a native wrote them. For other everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you start a formal email in Spanish?
faq.a: Use Estimado or Estimada followed by the person’s title and surname and a colon, for example Estimada Sra. Gómez:, then start your message on a new line.

faq.q: How do you end a formal email in Spanish?
faq.a: Atentamente is the most formal closing. Saludos cordiales and Un saludo are friendly and professional.

faq.q: How do you say “please find attached” in Spanish?
faq.a: Le adjunto… or Adjunto le envío… are the natural options. Avoid the literal Por favor encuentre adjunto.
